question: Which government power authorizes a municipality to enact zoning ordinances that regulate how land within its jurisdiction may be used?
choice_a: Police power -- the government's inherent authority to regulate private property and conduct for the public health, safety, morals, and general welfare
choice_b: Eminent domain -- the power to take private property for public use upon payment of just compensation
choice_c: Escheat -- the power to reclaim property when an owner dies leaving no will and no ascertainable heirs
choice_d: Taxation -- the power to levy charges against property to fund government operations
explanation: Zoning ordinances -- along with building codes, subdivision regulations, and similar land-use controls -- are a classic exercise of police power. Unlike eminent domain, no compensation is owed to an owner whose land is validly zoned, because the owner retains title and possession; the government is regulating use, not taking property.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls) -- the four government powers over land (police power, eminent domain, taxation, escheat) are foundational PSI national-portion content

question: A small retail shop has operated continuously in a certain location since before the surrounding area was rezoned to residential-only use. Although the shop no longer conforms to the current zoning classification, it is permitted to continue operating. This status is known as a:
explanation: A legal nonconforming use is a use that lawfully existed before a zoning change made it noncompliant, and that is allowed to continue under a grandfather clause. It typically cannot be expanded, and most ordinances terminate the protection if the use is abandoned for a set period or if the structure is destroyed beyond a stated percentage of its value.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: An owner's lot has an unusual shape that makes it impossible to meet the zoning ordinance's standard side-yard setback without an impractical loss of buildable area. The owner asks the zoning board for permission to build closer to the property line than the ordinance normally allows, based on this unique physical hardship. This form of individual relief from a dimensional zoning requirement is called a:
explanation: A variance is relief granted to an individual property owner from a specific, literal requirement of a zoning ordinance (commonly a setback, height, or lot-coverage rule) because strict application would create unnecessary and unique hardship. It is distinguished from a special use permit, which authorizes a particular use the ordinance already contemplates subject to conditions, and from rezoning, which changes the classification of the land itself.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A zoning ordinance does not generally permit religious institutions in a given district, but it lists certain uses -- including houses of worship -- that may be approved on a case-by-case basis if the applicant meets specified conditions (such as parking, buffering, or hours of operation). This type of government approval for an otherwise-restricted but ordinance-recognized use is called a:
choice_d: special use permit (also called a conditional use permit)
explanation: A special use (or conditional use) permit allows a use the zoning ordinance itself lists as potentially appropriate within a district, but only after government review confirms that stated conditions are satisfied. This differs from a variance, which grants relief from a dimensional requirement rather than authorizing a use category.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A city council rezones a single small parcel within an otherwise uniform residential neighborhood to allow a gas station, benefiting only that one landowner and bearing no rational relationship to the surrounding area's comprehensive plan. Courts frequently strike down this kind of arbitrary, isolated rezoning as invalid. It is known as:
explanation: Spot zoning is the rezoning of a small parcel in a way that is inconsistent with the surrounding area and the jurisdiction's comprehensive plan, typically for the benefit of a single owner rather than the public interest. Because zoning must be exercised for the general welfare, spot zoning that lacks a rational planning basis is a common ground for a successful legal challenge.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: Which government power allows a governmental body (or a private entity granted condemnation authority, such as a regulated utility or railroad) to take privately owned real property for a public use, provided the owner is paid just compensation?
explanation: Eminent domain is the government's constitutional power to take private property for public use so long as the owner receives just compensation, generally measured as the property's fair market value at the time of taking. This distinguishes it from police power (regulation without compensation) and from escheat and special assessments, which involve neither a forced taking of title nor a compensation requirement in the same sense.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls); just-compensation requirement traces to the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause (applied to the states via the Fourteenth Amendment) and is independently guaranteed under Michigan Constitution Art. 10, Sec. 2

question: In County of Wayne v. Hathcock, 471 Mich. 445 (2004), the Michigan Supreme Court overruled its own earlier Poletown Neighborhood Council v. City of Detroit (1981) decision. What did the Hathcock decision hold about the use of eminent domain in Michigan?
choice_a: Government may condemn any private property for any purpose so long as fair market value is paid, regardless of who ultimately receives title
choice_b: Local governments in Michigan no longer have eminent domain authority at all; only the state itself may condemn property
choice_c: Government generally may not condemn private property and transfer it to another private party solely for economic development, such as reducing unemployment or expanding the tax base -- "public use" does not include that kind of private economic benefit except in narrow, historically recognized circumstances
choice_d: Just compensation in Michigan is capped at the property's most recent assessed value for tax purposes
explanation: In Poletown (1981), the Michigan Supreme Court had allowed the City of Detroit to condemn an entire neighborhood and convey it to General Motors for a new assembly plant, reasoning that the resulting jobs and tax revenue served a public purpose. In Hathcock (2004), the court reversed course, holding that transferring condemned property to a private party purely for economic development does not satisfy the "public use" requirement of the Michigan Constitution, except in narrow situations such as takings for common carriers, highly regulated public utilities, or the elimination of genuine blight.
source_note: verified: County of Wayne v. Hathcock, 471 Mich. 445, 684 N.W.2d 765 (Mich. 2004), overruling Poletown Neighborhood Council v. City of Detroit, 410 Mich. 616 (1981); confirmed via live research (Michigan appellate case law, cross-checked against Michigan Bar Journal and Institute for Justice case summaries)

question: A county's new drainage project causes chronic flooding on a nearby landowner's property, substantially destroying its usable value, even though the county never filed a formal condemnation action or took title to the land. The landowner sues the county to recover compensation for this de facto taking. This type of owner-initiated claim is known as:
explanation: Inverse condemnation is a legal action brought by a property owner -- rather than the government -- alleging that government action has effectively taken or substantially damaged the owner's property without formal condemnation proceedings, entitling the owner to just compensation. It "inverts" the usual eminent domain process, in which government initiates the taking.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A property owner dies without a valid will (intestate) and a diligent search reveals no legally ascertainable heirs. Under the government power that prevents real property from being left ownerless, title to the property ultimately:
choice_b: is automatically taken by eminent domain
choice_c: is held indefinitely by the county recorder pending a future claim, with no transfer of title
choice_d: is divided among the deceased's most recent neighbors
explanation: Escheat is the government power under which title to real property reverts to the state when an owner dies intestate and leaves no heirs capable of taking title. It ensures that land is never left without a legal owner. Escheat is unrelated to eminent domain (a forced purchase for public use) or police power (regulation of existing owners).
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A county assessor determines the taxable value of every parcel in the jurisdiction and bills each owner a property tax rate applied against that value to fund general government services such as schools, police, and roads. A tax levied in proportion to a property's value in this way is called a(n):
choice_a: special assessment, which funds a specific local improvement benefiting only certain parcels
choice_b: ad valorem tax, and unpaid amounts typically create a tax lien on the property that takes priority over most other liens, including previously recorded mortgages
choice_c: documentary transfer tax, imposed only when title to the property changes hands
choice_d: escheat tax, imposed only on property that has reverted to the state
explanation: "Ad valorem" means "according to value" -- a general real property tax levied on all taxable parcels in proportion to assessed value, used to fund general government operations. Because governments rely on this revenue, unpaid ad valorem property taxes typically create a lien that has priority over virtually all other liens against the property, including mortgages recorded earlier in time -- an important exception to the usual "first in time, first in right" lien-priority rule.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A city installs new sidewalks and street lighting along one specific block and bills only the owners of the parcels fronting that block for the cost, in proportion to the benefit each parcel receives, rather than spreading the cost across the whole tax base. This targeted, benefit-based charge is called a:
explanation: A special assessment is a charge levied only against the specific properties that directly benefit from a local public improvement -- such as sidewalks, sewers, street paving, or lighting -- in proportion to the benefit conferred, unlike a general ad valorem tax, which is spread across the entire taxing jurisdiction to fund general government operations.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A developer records a deed restriction limiting all lots in a subdivision to single-family residential use only, even though the local zoning ordinance would otherwise allow duplexes on those same lots. A subsequent buyer wants to build a duplex, relying on the zoning ordinance. Which statement correctly describes how these two controls interact?
choice_a: Zoning always overrides a private deed restriction, so the buyer may build the duplex
choice_b: The deed restriction is automatically void because it conflicts with the zoning ordinance
choice_c: The buyer may choose to follow either control, whichever is more convenient
choice_d: The buyer must comply with whichever restriction is stricter; a valid, recorded private deed restriction can impose tighter limits on land use than public zoning allows, and both must be satisfied
explanation: Public land-use controls (zoning) and private land-use controls (deed restrictions, restrictive covenants) operate independently and both must generally be satisfied; compliance with zoning does not excuse a violation of a valid private restriction, and vice versa. Where the two conflict, the property owner must comply with whichever is more restrictive. Deed restrictions, once properly created and recorded, typically "run with the land" and bind subsequent owners even though they were not parties to the original agreement.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

question: A homeowners association (HOA) in a platted subdivision seeks to stop a homeowner from building a fence that violates the subdivision's recorded covenants, conditions, and restrictions (CC&Rs). Because the CC&Rs are a private land-use control rather than a government zoning ordinance, how does the HOA typically enforce them?
choice_a: The HOA (or another owner within the subdivision with standing) sues in civil court for an injunction and/or monetary damages -- CC&Rs are enforced through private civil litigation, not government zoning enforcement
choice_b: The HOA reports the violation to the municipal zoning board, which prosecutes it as a zoning code violation
choice_c: The HOA cannot take any enforcement action because CC&Rs are unenforceable once zoning is adopted for the area
choice_d: The state real estate licensing agency investigates and can suspend the homeowner's mortgage
explanation: Subdivision CC&Rs are private land-use controls, typically enforced by the developer, the HOA, or other lot owners through civil litigation seeking an injunction (to stop or reverse the violation) or damages, rather than through government zoning enforcement machinery. CC&Rs commonly also authorize the HOA to levy assessments and adopt bylaws governing common areas and architectural standards.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate principles (land use controls)

topic: Land Use Controls - Michigan Condominium Act
question: Under Michigan's Condominium Act (1978 PA 59, MCL 559.101-559.276), which condominium document is defined as the instrument that creates and records the condominium project, incorporating the bylaws and the condominium subdivision plan as attached exhibits, and that includes the legal description of the land and the designation of units served by limited common elements?
choice_b: The master deed, as defined at MCL 559.108
choice_d: The homeowners association's articles of incorporation
explanation: MCL 559.108 defines the "master deed" as the condominium document that records the project, with the bylaws and the condominium subdivision plan attached and incorporated by reference. The master deed must include an accurate legal description of the land in the project and must designate which units are served by, and define the rights in, each limited common element.
source_note: verified: MCL 559.108, Michigan Condominium Act (1978 PA 59), 'Master deed' defined -- confirmed via live research of Michigan Legislature statutory text

topic: Land Use Controls - Michigan Condominium Act
question: Under Michigan's Condominium Act, the administration of a condominium project -- including designation of who manages the project's affairs and requirements to keep detailed books and records of expenditures and receipts -- is governed by which recorded document, whose mandatory provisions cannot be eliminated by later amendment?
choice_b: The individual co-owner's unit deed only
choice_c: The bylaws, recorded as part of (or as provided in) the master deed under MCL 559.153, with certain mandatory provisions required by MCL 559.154
explanation: MCL 559.153 provides that administration of a Michigan condominium project is governed by bylaws recorded as part of, or as provided in, the master deed, and that an amendment to the bylaws may not eliminate the mandatory provisions required under MCL 559.154 (such as designating who administers the project and requiring detailed financial recordkeeping). Bylaw amendments must themselves be recorded with the register of deeds.
source_note: verified: MCL 559.153 (bylaws governing administration, recorded as part of master deed) and MCL 559.154 (mandatory bylaw provisions), Michigan Condominium Act (1978 PA 59) -- confirmed via live research of Michigan Legislature statutory text

topic: Land Use Controls - Michigan Condominium Act
question: Under Michigan's Condominium Act, a condominium unit's exclusive-use balcony -- reserved in the master deed for the use of only that unit's co-owner even though it is technically part of the shared building structure -- is best classified as which of the following?
choice_a: Part of the co-owner's individually deeded unit, with no association interest whatsoever
choice_b: Government-owned property held in trust for all residents of the municipality
choice_c: A nonconforming use that must eventually be removed
choice_d: A limited common element, defined under MCL 559.103 as a portion of the common elements reserved in the master deed for the exclusive use of fewer than all co-owners, as distinguished from general common elements appurtenant to two or more units
explanation: MCL 559.103 distinguishes "common elements" (portions of the condominium appurtenant to two or more units, or to one unit but subject to association control) from "limited common elements" -- a subset of the common elements that the master deed reserves for the exclusive use of less than all co-owners, such as a balcony, patio, or designated parking space serving only one unit. Limited common elements remain part of the condominium's common property but carry exclusive-use rights for a specific unit.
source_note: verified: MCL 559.103, Michigan Condominium Act (1978 PA 59), 'Common elements' and 'limited common elements' defined -- confirmed via live research of Michigan Legislature statutory text
